issues.legal_issue: An unauthorized administrative communication does not create an enforceable right to acquire public market property on a hire-purchase basis when the required institutional decision and approval are absent.
material_facts: The claimants were licensed traders who occupied shops, godowns, and sheds allotted to them on a rental basis and sought their transfer on a hire-purchase basis.
The governing law required the market committee to obtain the market board’s prior written approval and pass a prescribed resolution before transferring immovable property.
The board had not decided to transfer the property to the traders, and no document showed that it had authorized such a transfer.
A director’s letter referring to hire-purchase arrangements was not shown to have been authorized by the board or to have resulted in a board decision.
issues.conclusion: The claimants had no legal right to demand transfer of the shops, godowns, or sheds on a hire-purchase basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 12(1) of the U.P. Krishi Utpadan Mandi Adhiniyam, 1964, a market committee cannot transfer immovable property without the required resolution and the board’s prior written approval. Section 26-L does not confer on the director power to direct such transfers. An unauthorized letter that did not result in a board decision cannot establish an entitlement to transfer.

predicates.writ_claims_hire_purchase_transfer: A claimant seeks in a writ proceeding to compel transfer of public market premises on a hire-purchase basis.
predicates.director_communication_unapproved: An administrative communication about transferring the premises was not authorized by the body empowered to make the transfer decision.
predicates.no_board_transfer_decision: The body empowered to decide on transfer did not make a decision to transfer the premises to the claimants.

issues.definition: When a writ claimant seeks a hire-purchase transfer based only on an unauthorized administrative communication and the empowered body made no transfer decision, the claimant has no enforceable right to that transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A court does not substitute its preferred policy for a public authority’s choice about whether to lease or transfer its property unless the policy is shown to be unlawful or otherwise subject to judicial interference.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether public market premises should be leased to traders or transferred to them on a hire-purchase basis.
The authority maintained that its policy was to let the premises on rent and denied that it had promised to transfer them.
The claimants produced no document substantiating an assurance that the premises would be transferred.
The claimants did not establish that the authority’s policy was unlawful, arbitrary, discriminatory, or mala fide.
issues.conclusion: The court could not direct the authority to transfer the premises on a hire-purchase basis in place of its rental policy.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of policy choices is limited. Under Netai Bag v. State of West Bengal (2000) 8 SCC 262, State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal (1986) 4 SCC 566, BALCO Employees Union v. Union of India (2002) 2 SCC 333, and Federation of Railway Officers Association v. Union of India (2003) 4 SCC 289, a court does not choose what it considers a wiser or fairer policy; interference may be justified where a policy is contrary to law or the Constitution, arbitrary, irrational, discriminatory, mala fide, or an abuse of power.

predicates.policy_review_proceeding: A party asks a court in a proceeding to review a public authority’s policy choice.
predicates.public_property_disposition_policy: The policy choice concerns whether a public authority will lease or transfer property it owns or controls.
predicates.no_unlawfulness_or_arbitrariness_shown: The party challenging the policy does not establish that it is unlawful, arbitrary, irrational, discriminatory, mala fide, or an abuse of power.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a public property-disposition policy and no unlawfulness or arbitrariness is shown, the policy decision is not interfered with.

issues.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus cannot compel a public authority to transfer property when the authority has no applicable statutory duty to do so and the claimant has no legal right to require the transfer.
material_facts: The claimants sought a writ compelling the authorities to transfer the allotted premises on a hire-purchase basis.
The governing law did not impose a duty on the authorities to transfer the premises to the claimants.
The claimants had no legal right to require such a transfer because the empowered body had not decided to transfer the property.
issues.conclusion: The requested writ of mandamus could not be granted.
issues.legal_principle: The Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Cooperative Society Ltd. v. Sipahi Singh, AIR 1977 SC 2149, establishes that mandamus requires a statutory duty imposed on the authority and a corresponding legal right in the claimant. The applicable provisions did not impose a duty to make the claimed transfer, and the claimants had no corresponding right.

predicates.mandamus_claim: A claimant asks a court to compel a public authority to transfer property.
predicates.no_statutory_transfer_duty: The applicable law does not require the authority to make the transfer sought.
predicates.no_claimant_right_to_transfer: The claimant has no legal right to require the authority to make the transfer.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks mandamus to compel a property transfer but the law imposes no transfer duty and the claimant has no right to the transfer, mandamus is unavailable.
